newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Caterpillar Q4 EPS seen up 23 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Caterpillar Q4 EPS seen up 23 pct.

text.p: Caterpillar Inc is expected to post strong earnings per share gains for the fourth quarter of 1996, driven by improving margins.
Margin controls, as well as stronger international sales, could help gains continue into 1997, analysts said.

"The main thing to watch is that Cat's gross profit margin should be in the vicinity of 25 percent in 1997," said Barry Bannister, analyst at S.G. Warburg. "That is quite a leap from just five years ago...."

The mean estimate of 22 analysts surveyed by First Call was fourth quarter earnings of $1.88 a share, which would be up almost 23 percent from $1.53 a year ago. The 1997 mean estimate is $7.08 a share, up from an estimated $6.95 a share in 1996. In 1995, Caterpillar earned $5.72.
The Peoria, Illinois-based heavy equipment maker was expected to announce fourth quarter and full 1996 earnings Tuesday before the market opens.
One analyst who is well above consensus for 1997 sees modest sales improvements and modest margin controls helping Caterpillar post earnings of $8.25 a share in 1997.

That analyst, Alexander Blanton of Ingalls & Snyder Llc, said he expected gross margins to rise to 26 percent in 1997 from an estimated 25.4 percent in 1996, with a 4.7 percent increase in real sales and a two percent price increase on top of that.
"The emerging nations will do better," Blanton said of areas where Caterpillar could post sales gains.
Said Bannister: "It's still a macro story, in that you need to have European recovery from a slowdown in '96."
The company's aggressive share repurchase program should also help improve earnings per share.

One factor that still looms over Caterpillar is its labor situation. United Auto Workers members returned from a 16-month strike without a contract in 1995 and are still working under terms implemented in 1992.
But the company has contineud to post record earnings despite the labor troubles and analysts are skeptical the labor situation means much to Caterpillar's bottom line.

"That's up to the UAW," Blanton said when asked if Caterpillar would reach an accord with the union in 1997. "I don't know what they're going to do, but I don't think it really matters to the company."
